generatedProse.concept-context: Across any subject, you often start an essay or project facing a wide topic and no obvious structure. Visual mapping gives you a way in. You put the question at the centre and branch outward with ideas, points and examples, adding them before you judge them. Grouping the branches then turns a scatter of material into a clear structure you can write from.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students planning the same essay from a blank page.

Student A writes a quick list of points down the page, settles on the first three that seem usable, and starts drafting. The plan is done fast. But the list closed down early: Student A took the first ideas that came and never saw how the points might connect or which one was missing. The essay stays thin.

Student B puts the question in the centre of a page and branches outward, adding ideas, points and examples freely without judging them yet. With the map full, Student B groups the branches, names a few themes, and orders them into a plan. The same blank page has produced a richer, better-organised essay.

Both students planned the same essay. Only Student B used a method that generated ideas widely and then organised them, rather than settling on the first few.
generatedProse.summary: Creative methods give you a way into academic work when ideas are hard to find. A visual mapping method, such as a mind map, helps you generate ideas by branching from a central topic, and then organise them by grouping the branches into a structure. You can now use a mapping method, shape its output into a plan, and choose a method that fits the task. The next lesson widens this from one method to generating several approaches.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Student B do that organised the ideas, rather than only generating them?

items.text: Grouped related branches into themes and put the themes into an order to write from.
Wrote down more points than Student A did.
Chose the first three ideas and stopped.

feedback.correct: That's right. Grouping the branches into themes and ordering them is what organised Student B's ideas.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what turned the scatter of material into a structure.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B organised the ideas by grouping related branches into themes and ordering them into a plan. Writing more or drafting faster is not organising.
